sections.title: From What to How
learningObjectives: Recall MoRo's core identity from Module 1
Understand why navigation is the technology worth examining next
sections.content: Module 1 established what MoRo is: an autonomous mobile robot that navigates without fixed paths or floor markers. That claim raises an obvious question — how does it actually know where it is? This module answers that directly, covering the sensor technology and the localization process that together let MoRo move through a factory without floor tape or magnets, using a LiDAR map of the space.

keyTerms.note: An older category of automated vehicle that follows a fixed path, typically magnetic tape or a buried wire, requiring floor modification.

video.title: Maps, not tape in 30 seconds
video.transcript: Maps, not tape. How MoRo finds its way. LiDAR measures distance with laser light. It sees walls, machines, pillars and people. SLAM locates MoRo and builds the map at once. So no floor tape or magnets are needed. Glass and mirror-like surfaces can confuse LiDAR. If the layout changes, the map needs updating.

sections.title: LiDAR — How MoRo Senses Its Surroundings
learningObjectives: Define LiDAR and explain its basic operating principle
Understand what LiDAR can and cannot reliably detect
sections.content: LiDAR (Light Detection and Ranging) is a sensor that emits laser light and measures the time it takes to return after reflecting off a surface, calculating distance from that measurement. MoRo uses this continuously to detect walls, machines, pillars, and people around it. LiDAR has known physical limitations: it detects solid surfaces reliably, but struggles with transparent materials (glass) and very shiny or mirror-like surfaces, since these don't reflect the laser predictably back to the sensor. Very fine or low-profile objects at floor level are also harder to detect reliably than larger obstacles. Precise range and detection specifications for MoRo's LiDAR configuration are being confirmed against current hardware documentation and will be added once verified.

keyTerms.note: Light Detection and Ranging — a sensor that measures distance using reflected laser light.

sections.title: SLAM — Locating Itself While Mapping
learningObjectives: Define SLAM and its two component processes
Understand why SLAM enables navigation without fixed infrastructure
sections.content: SLAM (Simultaneous Localization and Mapping) is the process combining two tasks MoRo performs at once: localization (determining its own position) and mapping (building a representation of its surroundings). Neither happens in isolation — MoRo uses what it's mapped to figure out where it is, and uses its estimated position to keep refining the map. This is what eliminates the need for floor tape, magnetic strips, or any other physical infrastructure that older AGV systems required.

keyTerms.note: The combined process of determining one's own position while building a map of the environment, performed continuously and together.
Determining one's own position within a known or partially known environment.

sections.title: Positioning Accuracy
learningObjectives: Know MoRo's positioning accuracy by variant (about 10 mm for the A-250 and A-500, 20 mm for the A-1200)
Understand that accuracy differs across the product line
sections.content: Positioning accuracy is not identical across all three MoRo variants. The A-250 and A-500 are rated at ±10mm positioning accuracy; the A-1200 is rated at ±20mm — the larger variant's accuracy is intentionally wider, reflecting its different operating profile. This distinction matters operationally: don't assume the same precision applies uniformly across every unit on the floor without checking which variant you're working with.

keyTerms.note: How precisely MoRo can determine and maintain its actual physical position, expressed as a margin of error.

sections.title: Map Creation and Updates
learningObjectives: Understand the general process of building an initial map
Know that maps need updating when the factory layout changes
sections.content: Before MoRo operates independently in a space, an initial mapping pass is required — the unit is guided through the area to build its baseline map using LiDAR and SLAM. Once established, this map isn't permanent: if the factory layout changes (equipment relocated, new obstacles introduced), the map needs updating to reflect reality. The specific update cadence and process will be confirmed against DiFacto's operational guidance and added here once verified.

sections.title: What This Means for You
learningObjectives: Understand the practical implication of sensor-based navigation for floor personnel
Recognize what to be mindful of given LiDAR's known limitations
sections.content: Because MoRo's navigation depends on LiDAR detecting solid surfaces, be mindful of what it may not reliably register — transparent barriers, highly reflective surfaces, and very low-profile floor obstructions. This isn't a flaw to be anxious about; it's simply how the sensing technology works. Understanding the technology builds appropriate trust — not blind trust, not undue suspicion.

questions.question: What does LiDAR measure to determine distance?
options: The return time of reflected laser light
The strength of the magnetic field near the sensor
The echo time of sound waves bounced off surfaces
questions.feedback: Correct. LiDAR calculates distance from the return time of reflected laser light.

questions.question: What two things does SLAM do at the same time?
options: Works out MoRo's position and builds a map of its surroundings
Plans the route and charges the battery
Detects people and sounds the alarm
questions.feedback: Correct. SLAM is Simultaneous Localization and Mapping: working out where MoRo is and what is around it, both at once.

questions.question: Which type of surface is LiDAR least reliable at detecting?
options: Large machines with painted metal casings
Solid walls with a matte painted finish
questions.feedback: Correct. Transparent and highly reflective surfaces don't reflect laser light predictably.

questions.question: Two different MoRo variants work on your floor. What should you assume about their positioning accuracy?
options: It is identical on every unit
It may differ, so check which variant you are working with
The largest variant is the most precise
questions.feedback: Correct. Positioning accuracy is not identical across variants, so do not assume every unit is equally precise.

questions.question: A new rack is installed in an aisle MoRo uses. What does this mean for MoRo's map?
options: Nothing, because the map is permanent
It needs updating to match the new layout
The map updates only when MoRo is restarted
questions.feedback: Correct. The map is not permanent. If the layout changes, it needs updating.
